kp.k: Commoditisation and IT threaten traditional legal practice
kp.d: In this October 28, 2007 commentary, Giacalone endorses Richard Susskind’s forecasts from excerpts of his forthcoming book. Susskind predicts that commoditisation and information technology will reduce conventional lawyers’ prominence and displace outdated practice. These are prospective arguments about IT and smart systems, not measured findings about contemporary generative AI.
qs: This, I believe, is where we will be taken by two forces: by a market pull towards commoditisation and by pervasive development and uptake of information technology.

will determine that the legal world is over-resourced, it will increasingly drive out inefficiencies and unnecessary friction and, in so doing, we will indeed witness the end of outdated legal practice and the end of outdated lawyers.

kp.k: Tasks face substitution where systems perform equally well
kp.d: Susskind challenges lawyers to identify work that alternative methods could deliver faster, cheaper, more efficiently or to higher quality. His predicted substitution is conditional on systems and processes matching or exceeding lawyers’ performance, and encompasses advising, drafting, research and problem-solving rather than asserting the disappearance of all lawyers.
qs: what elements of their current workload could be undertaken differently — more quickly, cheaply, efficiently, or to a higher quality — using alternative methods of working.

is increasingly unlikely to tolerate expensive lawyers for tasks (guiding, advising, drafting, researching, problem-solving and more) that can equally or better be discharged, directly or indirectly, by smart systems and processes.

kp.k: Professional adaptation should replace exclusive claims to work
kp.d: Susskind argues that lawyers have no inherent entitlement to profit from law and recommends entrepreneurial redesign of services rather than protection of lawyer-exclusive work. Giacalone presents this as a public-interest alternative to professional protectionism.
qs: I do not believe lawyers are self-evidently entitled to profit from the law.

This series calls for the growth and the development of a legal profession not by ring-fencing certain categories of work as the exclusive preserve of lawyers; nor by encouraging cartel-like activity which discourages all but lawyers from engaging.
to find and embrace better, quicker, less costly, more convenient and publicly valued ways of working.

kp.k: Income and status concerns may obstruct reform
kp.d: Drawing on his stated three decades as a competition and consumer advocate, Giacalone doubts that the American profession will embrace Susskind’s challenge. He argues that threatened income and status encourage resistance, including among otherwise well-intentioned lawyers. This is his advocacy-based interpretation, supported in part by a quoted June 16, 2003 Illinois State Bar Association publication, rather than a systematic empirical finding.
qs: After three decades watching the legal profession in the USA from the perspective of a competition and consumer advocate, it is difficult to be optimistic that Susskind’s hoped-for introspection will yield progress rather than cartel-style roadblocks to change.
Good intentions of any one individual lawyer can be readily overwhelmed by the demands of partners (at work and home) to keep the income stream flowing.
the top concerns of the practicing bar are the economics of the practice and the image of the profession.

kp.k: Regulatory openness determines whether consumers benefit
kp.d: Giacalone proposes indicators for judging whether the American bar serves consumers or protects incumbents: expansion of court self-help, support for unbundling and price competition, narrower practice-of-law restrictions, and adoption of UK-style reforms including nonlawyer firms and improved discipline. He asks whether federal competition agencies will continue advocating narrower restrictions and whether state institutions will heed them; these are reform tests, not reported outcomes.
qs: are state court systems allowed to continue to expand their *pro se*/self-help facilities and services?
will the federal competition agencies (Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission)
for carving a narrow definition of the practice of law, and narrowing the scope of Unlawful Practice of Law statutes and regulations?
(improved disciplinary systems, entry of nonlawyer firms, etc.) proposed and adopted in the 50+ American legal jurisdictions?

kp.k: Technology-enabled self-help could address unmet civil legal needs
kp.d: Quoting the SHLEP About page, Giacalone reports that studies show 80% or more of poor and working-poor Americans’ legal needs are unmet, without supplying study methods, samples or dates in this document. He argues that computer technology, public literacy, public-oriented courts and lawyers offering discrete services could make self-help viable for most Americans’ legal problems. This is a conditional access-to-justice proposal, not a demonstrated intervention result.
qs: As a result, studies show that 80% or more of the legal needs of the poor and working poor currently are unmet in the United States, while even solid members of the middle class often cannot afford to hire a lawyer when a legal need arises.

By combining the existence of a literate public with the power of computer technology, with a judiciary that understands that our court system exists for the public (rather than for judges or the bar), and with lawyers willing and able to “unbundle” their services and perform discrete tasks for clients who want to handle their own legal matters, we can now make it possible for self-help to be a viable option for solving most of the legal problems of most Americans.

kp.k: Political advocacy should expand courthouse self-help
kp.d: Giacalone urges consumers and advocates to enlist legislators in supporting courthouse assistance for unrepresented litigants. He presents improved access as potentially beneficial both to the public and to politicians who support it, rather than treating technology alone as sufficient.
qs: When local politicians are smart enough to see the need for courthouse centers to help the unrepresented litigant, and when they are savvy enough to know that such support can have political advantages, we should see much more being done around the country to give the public the kind of accessible court system that they deserve.
Consumers and their advocates need to take this message to their legislators.

kp.k: Alternative billing should share efficiency benefits with clients
kp.d: Giacalone criticises consultants and commentators who promise premium pricing, greater lawyer income and fewer hours through branding and value billing. He argues that technological efficiency and excess supply should lower prices in a competitive market, and recommends evaluating alternative fees for fairness to clients as well as lawyers and firms. His marginal-cost expectation is explicitly conditional on competition, not an observed pricing result.
qs: Are they turning the problem of sky-high hourly-billing quotas into an excuse for using alternative billing methods that promise higher fees to lawyers?

those who sincerely want to fix what is wrong with hourly billing spend some serious time figuring out how the alternatives will result in fees (and a work environment) that are fair to lawyer, law firm and client
within an economy that, if working competitively, can be expected (due to technological breakthroughs and an excess of service providers) to drive prices down to their marginal costs.

kp.k: Hybrid advisers require deep multidisciplinary training
kp.d: In the November 5, 2007 update, Giacalone reports Susskind’s prediction that traditional black-letter lawyers will give way to multidisciplinary hybrid advisers as new ways of meeting demand eliminate inefficiencies. Susskind recommends substantive expertise in neighbouring fields and corresponding changes in law-school preparation, not merely relabelling existing legal practice.
qs: If lawyers want to re-invent themselves and carve out new multi-disciplinary roles that allow them to deliver new value, then their commitment to these neighbouring areas of expertise must be deep and our law schools should be gearing up accordingly.
new ways of satisfying legal demand will evolve and old inefficiencies will be eliminated.

kp.k: Legal knowledge engineers would package law into systems
kp.d: The November 5 update also quotes Susskind’s forecast of legal knowledge engineers who standardise and restructure legal knowledge for smart systems. Their envisaged users include lawyers, paralegals and laypeople, placing system-building alongside traditional advice and multidisciplinary practice as a future form of legal work.
qs: These are the highly skilled individuals who will be engaged in the jobs of standardising, systematising and packaging the law.
They will be the analysts who reorganise and restructure legal knowledge in a form that can be embodied in smart systems, whether for use by lawyers, para-legals or lay people.

kp.k: Solo autonomy does not guarantee technological adoption
kp.d: Giacalone quotes Grant Griffiths’s October 29, 2007 argument that solos and home-office practitioners adopt innovations faster because they control their own decisions. Giacalone qualifies that generalisation, pointing to older solos and financially or geographically constrained practitioners, and argues that solo practice amplifies individual circumstances rather than uniformly producing innovation.
qs: For that reason, we tend to adopt new advances in those areas, dare I say, quicker.
it is by no means a universal truth — at least not for older solos or for some of the more financially and geographically challenged members of our profession.
Being solo amplifies the individual’s personal traits and straits.

kp.k: Reader comments offer distinct market and jurisdictional qualifications
kp.d: Commenter Mike Young attributes commoditisation to excess supply and flexible, price-cutting practitioners, predicting pressure on smaller firms and justification of large-firm overhead; he recommends specialisation. Separately, Robert Precht’s November 2, 2007 comment contrasts Western debates over substitution with Japan’s perceived lawyer shortage and efforts to expand supply to help people assert rights against government and corporations. These are commenters’ assertions, not findings established by Giacalone.
qs: it will undercut small- to medium-size firms while pressuring large firms to justify high rates that pay for 1980s-style overhead and perqs.
To excel at law, one must develop a niche.

By contrast, here in Japan, there is a consensus that there are way too few lawyers. Efforts are underway to vastly increase the supply of lawyers. Why? To help Japanese people articulate and press rights, both against the government and large corporations.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source predicts reduced demand for traditional lawyers, new technology-oriented legal roles, downward price pressure, and expanded legal self-help through commoditisation and information technology.
pts.d: This is a 2007 discussion of information technology and smart systems, not specifically modern generative AI. Giacalone endorses and reproduces Richard Susskind's predictions that commoditisation and IT will reduce conventional legal advisers' prominence and displace outdated practices where systems can perform tasks equally well or better. These forecasts are Susskind's, as quoted and reported by Giacalone, rather than claims originating with the archive host. In the November 5 update, Susskind predicts multidisciplinary hybrid advisers and legal knowledge engineers who structure law for smart systems. Giacalone separately argues that technology, efficiencies and excess supply should lower prices in competitive markets, and that computer-supported self-help combined with unbundled lawyer assistance could address most Americans' legal problems. He warns that professional resistance and restrictions on competition could obstruct these changes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The predictions rest primarily on expert argument, Giacalone's professional observation, economic reasoning, and linked examples, rather than measured technology performance.
pts.d: Giacalone introduces Susskind through his earlier books and his role as IT Adviser to the Lord Chief Justice of England and Wales. The excerpts offer forward-looking arguments, not quantitative evidence of task substitution or productivity gains. Giacalone invokes three decades observing the US profession as a competition and consumer advocate and basic economic theory about efficiency and excess supply. Links concerning document assembly, self-help facilities, unbundling, LegalZoom and restrictions on nonlawyer assistance provide illustrative context; the supplied text does not present systematic outcome evaluations of them. A quoted SHLEP passage says studies show at least 80% of poor and working-poor Americans' legal needs are unmet, but does not identify those studies or their methods. That figure establishes the asserted access problem, not the demonstrated effectiveness of technological remedies.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The forecasts concern coming years and the twenty-first century without a precise displacement deadline; their operation depends on capable alternatives, competition, institutional support and professional adaptation.
pts.d: The main post is dated October 28, 2007, with subsequent updates. Susskind describes an evolving future rather than a dated forecast of all lawyers disappearing. Substitution is conditional on smart systems and processes discharging tasks equally well or better than expensive lawyers. His forecast of new hybrid roles requires deep expertise in neighbouring disciplines and corresponding law-school preparation. Giacalone's price prediction explicitly assumes a competitively functioning market. His claim that self-help is already potentially viable requires a literate public, computer technology, a public-oriented judiciary and lawyers willing to provide discrete services. He presents bar resistance, broad unauthorized-practice restrictions and barriers to nonlawyer entry as possible impediments. The linked question about lawyers existing in 100 years is a debate prompt, not a specific forecast adopted by Giacalone.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Traditional advisers face reduced demand; hybrid advisers and legal knowledge engineers gain roles; clients and unrepresented individuals could gain cheaper, more accessible services.
pts.d: Susskind's task-level forecast covers guiding, advising, drafting, researching and problem-solving, rather than identifying a particular firm-size segment or quantifying job losses. Lawyers could shift into multidisciplinary advice or the standardisation and packaging of legal knowledge. Lawyers, paralegals and laypeople are potential users of the resulting smart systems. Law schools would need to prepare students for new roles. Giacalone emphasises US legal consumers, particularly poor, working-poor and middle-class people unable to afford representation, as potential beneficiaries of technology-enabled self-help and unbundled services. Bar associations, courts, legislators and competition agencies affect whether those benefits become available. He also qualifies the suggestion that solo practitioners adopt innovations faster: individual traits, age and financial or geographic constraints make that uneven.
